newsitem.title: UKRAINE: German minister backs Ukraine reforms, Europe move.
newsitem.headline: German minister backs Ukraine reforms, Europe move.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel expressed his country's support for Ukraine's reforms and integration with Europe on Wednesday but made a plea for stable rules on foreign investment in the ex-Soviet republic.

"There is no alternative. Foreign investors and international financial organisations need clear and reliable conditions and signals for their activity," Kinkel said in a speech over lunch with Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko.
"Germany fully supports Ukraine in its policy of closeness and integration with European and trans-Atlantic structures," added Kinkel, on the second and final day of his visit to Kiev.

Last year, President Leonid Kuchma announced Ukraine's strategic aim to join the European Union and to become an associate member of the Western European Union. Kiev signed a charter on a special partnership with NATO earlier this month.
Germany is Ukraine's third biggest trading partner after Russia and Turkmenistan. Last year, trade stood at $1.7 billion. Germany is Kiev's second biggest investor after the United States.
According to German official data Bonn has provided Ukraine with 3.0 billion marks ($1.6 billion) in aid since Ukraine gained independence when the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991.
The results of an opinion poll published earlier this week said a majority of Ukrainians viewed Germany as an economic model for Ukraine, while the United States was viewed as the political model.
Kinkel, who also met Kuchma and new Prime Minister Valery Pustovoitenko, indicated Germany's strategy was to strike a balance between Russia and Ukraine.

"For us, the Germans, there have always been two great capitals in eastern Europe -- Moscow and Kiev. Ukraine has its special place and no one should consider it a country in the shadow of other large neighbours," Kinkel said.
Kinkel also made a plea that Ukraine not be turned into a "buffer zone" between Russia and the West, particularly with the expanded NATO defence alliance.
Kinkel said Kuchma promised to return a Lutheran church, located only a few dozens metres from the president's headquarters, to Ukraine's German community of about 40,000.

Kinkel and Udovenko told a joint news conference the two sides had agreed to set up a special body to deal with the exchange of cultural artefacts, some taken during the Nazi occupation of Ukraine in 1941-44, others taken by the Red Army from Germany.

"Here there are some problems," Udovenko said. "Germany has already returned some things, taken from Ukraine, to Russia or the former Soviet Union. We are asking Germany to tell us which masterpieces went to Moscow."
Memories of World War Two are still much alive in Ukraine where about five million local people died as a result of the conflict. ($ = 1.837 German Marks)
